metadata.title: GDP per Energy Use at the Global Level
metadata.description: The variable "GDP/unit of energy use" measures the economic efficiency of a country or region's energy use. In other words, it represents the economic value generated per unit of energy consumed. This metric is calculated as the ratio of GDP to total energy consumption. The formula to calculate "GDP/unit of energy use" is: GDP per unit of energy use = GDP / Energy Consumption. Where: GDP is the total value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given period, usually expressed in US dollars or another local currency; Energy Consumption is the total amount of energy used, expressed in units such as Joules, Terajoules, or equivalents in tons of oil (toe). This indicator is useful for assessing how efficiently an economy uses energy to produce economic value. A higher "GDP/unit of energy use" value indicates greater energy efficiency, as more economic value is produced per unit of energy consumed.

metadata.title: Redefining Processing Efficiency with In-Memory Computing Architecture
metadata.description: In-memory computing offers a transformative solution to address the bottlenecks of conventional computing architectures, were frequent data transfer between memory and processors limits performance. This study presents the design and evaluation of an in-memory computing architecture aimed at significantly reducing latency, enhancing energy efficiency, and increasing throughput by performing computations directly within memory arrays. By embedding logic functions alongside memory components, the proposed architecture achieves notable improvements in computational efficiency. Experimental results reveal that the architecture reduces latency by up to 43.33%, with tasks such as matrix multiplication demonstrating a decrease from 450 microseconds to 275 microseconds. Energy consumption is reduced by over 40%, as evidenced by neural network inference requiring only 7.2 joules compared to 12.5 joules in baseline systems. Furthermore, architecture enhances throughput by up to 52%, with AI model training achieving 1,520,000 operations per second compared to 1,000,000 in traditional architectures. These results establish the potential of in-memory computing to redefine conventional processing paradigms, delivering high-speed, energy-efficient computations for applications in AI, machine learning, and other data-intensive domains.

metadata.title: Hydrogen Recovery without Bulk Transport: A Dynamic Subsea Capture Approach
metadata.description: This study introduces a dynamic subsea capture framework for hydrogen recovery that departs from conventional production routes based on electrolysis and thermochemical conversion. Instead of generating hydrogen through energy-intensive bond dissociation, the proposed approach recovers hydrogen-bearing fluid through passive, flow-induced capture within a distributed environment. The system consists of a stationary or semi-stationary subsea unit equipped with controllable lateral openings and a sensor-guided control scheme. Relative motion is provided by ambient currents and, when needed, by short-range surface vessel movement over distances on the order of 50–100 meters. During each capture cycle, lateral openings are exposed to the surrounding flow for a short interval, allowing the chamber to fill under natural pressure and velocity conditions. The openings are then sealed and the cycle is repeated. This replaces continuous pumping and long-distance transport  with discrete, geometry-driven capture events. First-order analysis indicates that the energy required per kilogram of hydrogen is on the order of 10⁶ to 10⁷ joules, substantially lower than the approximately 2×10⁸ joules per kilogram, typically associated with water electrolysis. The resulting regime is primarily capture-limited, with performance governed by local concentration, flow conditions, and capture efficiency. The framework is particularly relevant in subsea environments where hydrogen-bearing species such as hydrogen sulfide are spatially distributed. Rather than targeting isolated reservoirs, the system performs repeated local sampling and accumulates product over time. By aligning the design with ambient hydrodynamics, the approach minimizes external energy input and simplifies system architecture. While feasibility is site-dependent, the results establish a physically consistent and scalable basis for low-energy subsea hydrogen recovery via dynamic capture.

Department of Energy and Power Engineering, School of Mechanical and Power Engineering, Henan Polytechnic University, 2000 Century Avenue, Jiaozuo, Henan, 454000, P.R. China

Contributor: Junjie Chen, ORCID: 0000-0001-5055-4309, E-mail address: komcjj@gmail.com

 

Specific heat is the quantity of heat required to raise the temperature of one gram of a substance by one Celsius degree. The units of specific heat are usually calories or joules per gram per Celsius degree. For example, the specific heat of water is one calorie (or 4.186 joules) per gram per Celsius degree. The Scottish scientist Joseph Black, in the 18th century, noticed that equal masses of different substances needed different amounts of heat to raise them through the same temperature interval, and, from this observation, he founded the concept of specific heat. Measurements of specific heats of substances allow calculation of their atomic weights.

metadata.title: ERA-5 Hydrometeorological Variables Daily – Verbier, Switzerland
metadata.description:
ERA-5 Hydrometeorological Variables Daily – Verbier, Switzerland

 

The dataset contains hydrometeorological variables from the ERA5-Land dataset, covering the period from January 10, 2023, to August 29, 2024.

It is provided in CSV format and includes the following variables:

  • date: The date of observation (format: DD-MM-YY).
  • dewpoint_temperature_2m: Dewpoint temperature at 2 meters above the surface (Kelvin).
  • runoff_sum: Total runoff (surface + subsurface) (meters).
  • skin_temperature: Temperature of the land surface (Kelvin).
  • snow_cover: Percentage of land covered by snow (%).
  • snow_depth: Snow depth (meters).
  • snow_depth_water_equivalent: Equivalent water content of snow depth (meters).
  • snowfall_sum: Total snowfall  (meters).
  • snowmelt_sum: Total snowmelt  (meters).
  • sub_surface_runoff_sum: Total subsurface runoff (meters).
  • surface_net_solar_radiation_sum: Total net solar radiation received at the surface (Joules per square meter).
  • surface_net_thermal_radiation_sum: Total net thermal radiation at the surface (Joules per square meter).
  • surface_runoff_sum: Total surface runoff (meters).
  • temperature_2m: Air temperature at 2 meters above the surface (Kelvin).
  • total_precipitation_sum: Total precipitation (meters).

The reference dataset is: "ERA5-Land Daily Aggregated - ECMWF Climate Reanalysis" 

More details for the reference dataset can be found at: https://doi.org/10.24381/cds.68d2bb30
